messages.body_plain:
Hi,

The version prior to the 0.9.x series had widths and heights, where
one could conveniently indicate:

    facet_grid (pane ~ ., scale='free_y', heights=c(2,1))

Indicating that the 1st facet is 2x larger then the second.

I want to be able to have a vertically facetted graph, with one pane
2x as large as the other.   This does not relate to the range of the
data series being rendered in each pane, rather is for purposes of
being able to put more focus visually on one of the facets.

This sort of scaling of facets (or timeseries rendering panes) is very
common in financial applications, where we want our main panel, say,
for price series to occupy a larger vertical space and have 1/2 or
1/3rd's sized panes with indicators below.

Is there some way to get this behavior?   Here is a mockup example:

	x <- 1:1000
	y1 <- cumsum(rnorm(1000))
	y2 <- diff(y1) * 1000

	data <- rbind (
		data.frame (x = x, y=y1, what='price', pane='price'),
		data.frame (x = x[-1], y=y2, what='dp', pane='indicators'))

        ggplot() +
		geom_line (aes(x=x, y=y, colour=what), data=data) +
		facet_grid (pane ~ ., scale='free_y', heights=c(2,1)) +
		theme_bw()

This ran previously, but now will only run without the heights
parameter.   Note that my real usage is more complex that this, where
there are multiple series in a pane and with different geometries.

Thanks in advance.

Jonathan

After discussing the resulting plot with my colleagues, I was asked to make the "connecting part" in a lighter colour than the bars. So I tried to overlay a bar plot onto the area plot created the way Winston suggests.

ggplot(df2, aes(x=xvarn, y=value, fill=groups, width=0.3)) +
  geom_area(colour="grey") +
  scale_fill_hue(c=45, l=80) +
  geom_bar(position="stack", stat="identity") +
  scale_fill_hue(l=40) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks=1:max(df2$xvarn), labels=levels(df2$xvarn))

This didn't work, as this approach would have required different colour scales, which according to Brandon's recent answer to Roey is not possible in ggplot2. Instead, Brandon suggested to overlay plots with grid, so that's what I tried next:

library("gridExtra")

df3 <- df2[1:(nrow(df2)/2),]  # remove duplicates for the bar plot

vp1 <- viewport(width=1, height=1, x=0.5, y=0.515)  # create a viewport of the same size and position as the plot area

p1 <- ggplot(df2, aes(x=xvarn, y=value, fill=groups)) +
  geom_area(colour="grey") +
  scale_fill_hue(c=45, l=80)

p2 <- ggplot(df2, aes(x=xvarn, y=value, fill=groups, width=0.3)) +
  geom_bar(position="stack", stat="identity") +
  scale_fill_hue(l=40) +
  opts(
    panel.background=theme_rect(fill="transparent", colour=NA),
    plot.background=theme_rect(fill="transparent", colour=NA)) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks=1:max(df2$xvarn), labels=levels(df2$xvarn))

p1
print(p2, vp=vp1)

Fortunately, the principle worked. Unfortunately, the result isn't perfect. The bars are slightly higher than the area height, and the y-values as well as the legend are slightly shifted. I tried ylim(0, 55) to fix the y-scale, but it didn't help. Does anyone have an idea what I could do to get a precise overlay?

messages.body_plain:
Thanks (yes Kohske, was the one who originally provided this), !   Would be nice to find an acceptable way to get this in as a permanent feature.

I remember that there was some disagreement as to whether this feature should be allowed in the context of a grammar for graphics, in that an artificial scaling does not match 1:1 with the actual range.    On the other hand, by using the default equal-sized facets with scale='free_y' or scale='free_x', we have a disconnect between size and domain / range.

Hence, if we allow what is currently supported, adding in this flexibility is no worse conceptually.

messages.subject: R development master class: NYC June 21-22, Bay Area June 28-29
messages.subject_clean: R development master class: NYC June 21-22, Bay Area June 28-29
messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

I'm going to be teaching an R development master classes in NYC June
21-12 and in the Bay Area June 28-29. The basic idea of the class is
to help you write better code, focused on the mantra of "do not repeat
yourself". In day one you will learn powerful new tools of
abstraction, allowing you to solve a wider range of problems with
fewer lines of code. Day two will teach you how to make packages, the
fundamental unit of code distribution in R, allowing others to save
time by allowing them to use your code.

To get the most out of this course, you should have some experience
programming in R already: you should be familiar with writing
functions, and the basic data structures of R: vectors, matrices,
arrays, lists and data frames. You will find the course particularly
useful if you're an experienced R user looking to take the next step,
or if you're moving to R from other programming languages and you want
to quickly get up to speed with R's unique features. You can see the
material we covered last time at http://bit.ly/odi3ai.

Both days will incorporate a mix of lectures and hands-on learning. Expect to
learn about a topic and then immediately put it into practice with a small
example. Plenty of help will be available if you get stuck. You'll receive a
printed copy of all slides, as well as electronic access to the slides, code
and data. The material covered in the course is currently being turned into a
book: you can access the current draft at http://bit.ly/dDv5rt.

To see prices, locations and register, please see:
http://bit.ly/lTft9e. Early bird discounts available until May 31, and
limited discounts for students (66% off) and academics (33% off) are
available - please contact me for details.

Regards,

Hadley

--
Assistant Professor / Dobelman Family Junior Chair
Department of Statistics / Rice University
http://had.co.nz/

ggpairs( test_ggally_data )

The reason I don't want to use na.omit is that I am comparing a bunch
of datasets which each have different values missing.

Presumably this should be easy to fix?

I hope this is the right mailing list for the post.

Thanks
Edward

messages.subject: Re: watermark
messages.body_plain:
Hi:

I don't have any direct experience with this sort of thing, but you
should be able to use something like annotation_raster() or
annotation_custom() [both new in ggplot2-0.9.0] as an initial
background layer if your watermark is a graphic. However, neither
function seems to have the option to set alpha transparency for the
input graphic, so you'd need to do that in advance. Whether this is
'better' than your approach is for you to decide - if your actual
watermark is a text string, then I see no reason to deviate from your
current method.

If you have a solid graphical object that you want for a background,
one way to fake transparency, I guess, would be to use one of the
above as the first layer in the ggplot2 graph, and then overlay it
with a geom_rect() at full size in a solid color with alpha
transparency before adding anything else. You could write a function
to do that.

A couple of examples of the use of the aforementioned annotation
functions are in the ggplot2-0.9.0 transition guide, section 4:
http://cloud.github.com/downloads/hadley/ggplot2/guide-col.pdf

HTH,
Dennis

messages.subject: Re: Package for using system fonts in R graphics
messages.subject_clean: Package for using system fonts in R graphics
messages.body_plain:
I've modified the extrafont package to support font packages -- that is R packages that contain font files in a particular directory structure. This should make it easy to distribute fonts on CRAN.

I made a package with the Computer Modern fonts (with symbols) here:
  https://github.com/wch/fontcm/

Installation is straightforward. You'll first need a new version of the extrafont package.

library(devtools)
install_github('extrafont', 'wch')
library(extrafont)

install_github('fontcm', 'wch')
font_install('fontcm')
# When fontcm is on cran, font_install will download from CRAN, install, and
# register the font with extrafont.

# This will show the registered fonts
fonts()

The fontcm github page shows how to generate the PDF that I've attached. The first page uses R's default fonts, and the second page uses Computer Modern.

One more thing: I've removed extrafont's dependency on the external program ttf2pt1, by including the source code, which gets compiled on install. This means that you need a build environment to install extrafont (until it's on CRAN with precompiled packages).

-Winston

messages.body_plain:
Hm, there might be a drawback to installing the fonts using font packages with extrafont (as opposed to installing the font on the OS, and them importing into extrafont).

If the fonts are installed only via a font package, then people will be able to use the fonts for PDFs and embed them. But then they won't be able to see the fonts for on-screen graphics (which uses fonts from the OS) or for PNG output. For example, when I use CM fonts via the cmfont package, I can only use them in PDFs right now -- they won't show on screen or in a PNG. But maybe (at least for PNG), that's something that can be worked around.

-Winston

Hi,

You can define a print method for gtable that does the same thing as
print.ggplot,

print.gtable = function (x, newpage = is.null(vp), vp = NULL, ...)
{
    if (newpage)
        grid.newpage()
        if (is.null(vp)) {
        grid.draw(x)
    }
    else {
        if (is.character(vp))
            seekViewport(vp)
        else pushViewport(vp)
        grid.draw(x)
        upViewport()
    }
    invisible(data)
}

HTH,

> Hm, there might be a drawback to installing the fonts using font packages with extrafont (as opposed to installing the font on the OS, and them importing into extrafont).
>
> If the fonts are installed only via a font package, then people will be able to use the fonts for PDFs and embed them. But then they won't be able to see the fonts for on-screen graphics (which uses fonts from the OS) or for PNG output. For example, when I use CM fonts via the cmfont package, I can only use them in PDFs right now -- they won't show on screen or in a PNG. I have data grouped by two factors, let's say gear and carb (see below).
To connect the points per group, I can either use

group=carb

group=gear

But what I need is something like group=c(carb + gear) to connect only the dots that have both factors in common.

I could create a new column, but there must be another way to do this...
Many thanks
- Christian

mtcars$gear = factor(mtcars$gear)
mtcars$carb = factor(mtcars$carb)

ggplot(mtcars) +
aes(hp,disp)+
aes(shape = gear) +
aes(color = carb) +
aes(group=carb) +
geom_point()+
geom_line()

messages.subject: Re: grouping by two factors (geom_line)
messages.body_plain:
You can use interaction(), like this:

mtcars$gear = factor(mtcars$gear)
mtcars$carb = factor(mtcars$carb)

ggplot(mtcars, aes(x=hp, y=disp, shape=gear, colour=carb)) +
    geom_point() +
    geom_line(aes(group=interaction(carb,gear)))

-Winston

messages.body_plain:
Hi:

I had to modify your data a bit because you had no observations for
minb, but I got something, at least. The problem does raise the
question of why there is no equivalent labeller = argument in
facet_wrap(), which would be better for your purposes IMO, but to get
expressions in strip labels, you currently have to use facet_grid().
Starting with your input data frame martindf,

mlabels <- levels(martindf$variable2)  # hold quoted expressions in a vector
martindfmelt <- melt(martindf, id = c('Treatment', 'variable'),
measure.vars = 'value')
names(martindfmelt) <- c('Treatment', 'variable1', 'variable2', 'value')
# This is a one-level factor that is unneeded, so get rid of it
martindfmelt$variable2 <- NULL
# Recreate the factor variable whose labels are quoted expressions
martindfmelt$variable <- factor(martindfmelt$variable1, labels = mlabels)

ggplot(martindfmelt, aes(x=Treatment, y=value)) +

   geom_boxplot(aes(fill=Treatment), notch=FALSE) +
   stat_summary(fun.y=mean, geom="point", shape=5,  size=2) +

   opts(legend.position="none",
        axis.title.x = theme_blank(),
        plot.title = theme_text(size=14, lineheight=.8, face="bold"),
        strip.background = theme_blank(),
        axis.title.x = theme_blank(),
        axis.text.x = theme_blank())  +

   scale_fill_brewer(type="seq", palette="Blues") +

   facet_grid(variable ~ ., scale="free_y", labeller=label_parsed)

Dennis

messages.subject: Re: Package for using system fonts in R graphics
messages.subject_clean: Package for using system fonts in R graphics
messages.body_plain:
For those who are still following along... On the advice of Paul Murrell, I've renamed the package 'fonts', and modified it so that requires a second package, 'fontsdb'. The fontsdb package is basically an empty package that contains the database.

Previously, when the database was stored in the fonts package, a re-installation or update of fonts would also delete the database. Separating the code and the database into two packages makes it possible to update the code without deleting the database.

Instructions are here: https://github.com/wch/fonts
The only real change is that you need to install fontsdb. Once it's on CRAN, the installation of fontsdb should be automatic.

-Winston

messages.body_plain:
On 5/25/2012 2:40 PM, Jeroen Ooms wrote:
> One of my customers insists on displaying the day of week somehow on the X
> axis on the timeseries plot. The dow is particulary important to them. Is
> there an easy way to accomplish this on a plot like e.g. this:
>
> dates<- as.Date(Sys.time()) - 10:1
> values<- 5 + cumsum(rnorm(10));
> mydata<- data.frame(dates, values);
> ggplot(aes(x=dates, y=values), data=mydata) + geom_bar(stat="identity");
>

Use the labels argument of scale_x_date; %a gives the abbreviated
weekday, $A, the full one:

ggplot(aes(x=dates, y=values), data=mydata) +
   geom_bar(stat="identity") +
   scale_x_date(labels=date_format("%a"))

or for an example of extremely verbose labels:

ggplot(aes(x=dates, y=values), data=mydata) +
   geom_bar(stat="identity") +
   scale_x_date(labels=date_format("%A, %B %d, %Y"))

--
Brian S. Diggs, PhD
Senior Research Associate, Department of Surgery
Oregon Health & Science University

messages.body_plain:
I think you want to add the points "geom" (appropriately given by  geom_point()) but with categorial variables that's sometimes prone to overplotting so I think the standard recommendation is geom_jitter()

With a built in data set something like

 ggplot(aes(y = price, x = cut, fill = color), data = diamonds) + geom_boxplot() + geom_jitter(alpha = I(1/100))

I added alpha because there are so many points for this data set it's necessary: it's a judgement call on yours.

Hope this helps,
Michael

messages.subject: Re: ggplot2: boxplot, with observation scatter plot.
messages.subject_clean: ggplot2: boxplot, with observation scatter plot.
messages.body_plain:
Hi:

Michael's advice is sound when you have a large data frame. If you have a relatively small one, an alternative to jittering is geom_dotplot(), new to version 0.9.0. Here's an example, taken from the 0.9.0 transition guide:

ggplot(mtcars, aes(x = factor(vs), y = mpg)) +
   geom_boxplot(aes(fill = factor(vs)), alpha = 0.3,
               outlier.color = NA) +
   geom_dotplot(binaxis = "y", stackdir = "center",
              position = "dodge", colour = "blue", fill = "blue") +
   labs(x = "vs", y = "mpg", fill = "vs")

If your boxplot contains outside values that are individually plotted, it's not a particularly good idea to add jittering alone because the outside values will be duplicated and jittered, making them appear to be twice as numerous as they really are. One workaround is to 'blank out' the outside values with 'outlier.color = NA', which is done above, recognizing that any value outside the extent of the whiskers in either direction is an outside value.

geom_dotplot() will also work with large data, but you will probably need to be careful about the widths of the stacked points as well as their size. Start with the defaults, as they are true to the intentions of the developer of the method; if they need to be modified, then consult the help page, which has a number of good examples.

HTH,
Dennis

messages.subject: Re: Display day of week on date axis
messages.subject_clean: Display day of week on date axis
messages.body_plain:
On 05/25/2012 05:40 PM, Jeroen Ooms wrote:
> One of my customers insists on displaying the day of week somehow on the X
> axis on the timeseries plot. The dow is particulary important to them. Is
> there an easy way to accomplish this on a plot like e.g. this:
>
> dates<- as.Date(Sys.time()) - 10:1
> values<- 5 + cumsum(rnorm(10));
> mydata<- data.frame(dates, values);
> ggplot(aes(x=dates, y=values), data=mydata) + geom_bar(stat="identity");
>

Try this:
-------------------------
require(ggplot2)
require(scales)

dates <- as.Date(Sys.time()) - 10:1
values <- 5 + cumsum(rnorm(10));
mydata <- data.frame(dates, values);

ggplot(aes(x=dates, y=values), data=mydata) + geom_bar(stat="identity")+
scale_x_date(labels=date_format("%A\n%b %d"));
-------------------------

Look at "?strftime" for all of the date format options. I added the "\n"
to split the date into to lines.

The following link helped me figure this out:
http://stackoverflow.com/questions/10576095/formatting-dates-with-scale-x-date-in-ggplot2

Jason

Hi,

If I understand your objection, it's more clearly reflected in this:

ggplot(aes(y = price, x = cut, fill = color), data = dia.DE) +   geom_boxplot() + geom_jitter(aes(color = color))

which shows that some of the blue dots wind up over the red boxplot and vice-versa [See attached graph1.pdf]

To get rid of this, you can reduce the width of the jittering to zero like this:

ggplot(aes(y = price, x = cut, fill = color), data = dia.DE) +   geom_boxplot() + geom_jitter(aes(color = color), position = position_jitter(width = 0))

[Producing graph2.pdf]

It seems that by default, ggplot2 does not seem to want to line up the points with the center of their boxplot (if it did, then you could just do a slight jitter of width no more than the boxplot and there wouldn't be any "traitors") but I don't know how to make it do so. Hopefully a ggmaster can chime in about how to do so, it does seem like a reasonable thing to ask.

Hope this helps,
Michael

messages.subject: Re: ggplot2: boxplot, with observation scatter plot.
messages.subject_clean: ggplot2: boxplot, with observation scatter plot.
messages.body_plain:
Hi:

This type of graphic, which has come up in this group several times in the past, illustrates one of the limitations of the grammar of graphics. In this example, boxplots are dodged by color within cut by default [on the geom_boxplot() help page, it is documented that mapped aesthetics, when factors, are 'automatically dodged' (see the examples section). The desire is to dodge the points in the same way *and* to jitter them. The problem is that both dodging and jitter are position adjustments, and only one is allowed - in other words, it's a nontrivial balancing act to get the two working in concert and it depends on the configuration of the graph. What works in one example may not map to another.

In a fairly simple case, you can get away with using position_jitter(); here's an example from the 0.9.0 transition guide that should work in 0.8.9 as well:

ggplot(mtcars, aes(x = factor(vs), y = mpg)) +
geom_boxplot(aes(fill = factor(vs)), alpha = 0.3,

                     outlier.colour = NA) +
geom_point(position = position_jitter(width = 0.05),

                  colour = "blue", fill = "blue") +
labs(x = "vs", y = "mpg", fill = "vs")

However, if you translate this to the present example, it doesn't work because the points are jittered relative to the levels of cut, not to the levels of color nested within cut. The 'automatic' dodging of the levels of color within cut that takes place in geom_boxplot() does not transfer to geom_point(). A (single) position adjustment of points is allowed; one that works (with a little tweaking of the width) is the following:

set.seed(1410)
dsmall <- diamonds[sample(nrow(diamonds), 100), ]
dia.DE <- dsmall[(dsmall$color=="D"|dsmall$color=="E")
                 & (dsmall$cut=="Ideal"|dsmall$cut=="Premium"|dsmall$cut=="Very Good"),]

ggplot(dia.DE, aes(y = price, x = cut, fill = color)) +
    geom_point(aes(colour = color), position = position_dodge(width = 0.75)) +
    geom_boxplot(alpha = 0.2, outlier.colour = NA)

If you replace geom_point() with geom_jitter(), the same plot should obtain, as geom_jitter() will ignore the position = position_dodge() argument. You can dodge or jitter, but you can't dodge _and_ jitter.

In 0.9.0, geom_dotplot() has a dodge = argument that allows one to specify the dodging variable; see the examples in section 3.3 of the transition guide for some illustrations as well as the geom_dotplot() help page:
http://cloud.github.com/downloads/hadley/ggplot2/guide-col.pdf

One approach to this problem using geom_dotplot() is the following:

# 0.9.0+ only:
ggplot(dia.DE, aes(y = price, x = cut, fill = color)) +
     geom_boxplot(alpha = 0.2, outlier.colour = NA) +
     geom_dotplot(aes(colour = color), binaxis = 'y',
                  stackdir = 'centerwhole', position = 'dodge')

Unfortunately, the center of the point stacks doesn't align perfectly with the whiskers of the box plots in this example. It's possible that default dodging width differs between geom_boxplot() and geom_dotplot(). Winston or someone else might be able to provide a better selection of arguments that gets the alignment right - I haven't been able to figure it out yet despite several guesses that didn't work.

If some enterprising soul is looking for a geom to create, this would be a good candidate :)

Dennis

Add the argument hjust = 0 in the annotate() call. Here's an example

messages.subject: Re: New theme system
messages.body_plain:
On 5/28/2012 10:07 PM, Winston Chang wrote:
> Hi everyone -
>
> I've been working on the new theme system, based off the ideas Hadley
> posted a while back. I think it's to the point where it's ready for some
> feedback. Check it out and let me know if you have any comments or
> suggestions:
>   https://github.com/wch/ggplot2/wiki/New-theme-system
>
> -Winston
>

I've just read the wiki page; I haven't looked at the code or even tried
installing it (yet). But I wanted to give some feedback:

The first thing, which I was VERY happy to see, was that you have a
backwards compatibility layer with deprecation messages. Hopefully the
message will point to the new (element_) function as well as a
transition-guide like resource (even that wiki page would be good).

I also like the element_*() renaming; the theme prefix meant two
different things, and that confusion has been eliminated.

I know that inheritance and single attribute updating were important
goals for the new design, so it is good to see that in there. A nice way
of specifying relative sizes is a nice addition. Gaining independent
control over x and y axis attributes is good. Perhaps that can be
further extended by having separate x/y versions of axis.ticks,
axis.ticks.length, axis.ticks.margin, and axis.line.

I am also glad that the implementation was not the start of the
description and that (it seems) the requirement drove the
implementation, and not the implementation driving the requirements.

Does rel() work only with font sizes, or could it (does it) work with
any numerical size. I'm thinking in particular margin/padding. Or any unit.

In terms of the inheritance structure:
* could legend.text and legend.title both inherit off of something off
of text? The obvious name would be legend.text, but that doesn't work
here since it is already being used.
* Can the margins (legend.margin, panel.margin, axis.ticks.margin,
plot.margin) inherit off a single margin, and maybe even use rel?
* Should there be some sort of relationship between segment and line?
They both have colour, size, and linetype.  I'm thinking segment
inherits from line.
* There are two align's and a justification (legend.justification,
legend.title.align, legend.text.align). I'm not sure what each take and
whether they could be related (in an inheritance way) to each other.
* What is the difference between legend.direction and legend.box? Both
take "horizontal" or "vertical" as values.
* Should the title text really be part of the theme? As I think about
the themes, it seems like it shouldn't. If not, then there is the
problem of where to put it. It is most similar to the labels of the
scales, but it is really not a scale. Short of just making a dedicated
function for it, or just putting it into labs(), I'm not sure what to do
with it.
* The only other elements that don't inherit from anything are:
axis.ticks.length, legend.position, title, legend.direction, legend.box.
I think that is fine; the first is a unit, but doesn't really relate to
anything; maybe to the margin sizes if that becomes a set. The three
legend bits are their own thing, and title is just a string.

Is precedence well defined for things like:

opts(axis.text = element_text(size=rel(0.5)),
      axis.text = element_text(size=4))

That is, will it work and will it give a consistent result?

Rather than modifying a theme directly as a list, why not utilize the
existing opts() infrastructure for assignment? or update?

mytheme <- theme_grey()

mytheme <- update(mytheme, opts(text = element_text(family="Times",
face="plain", colour="red", size=16, hjust=0.5, vjust=0.5, angle=0,
lineheight=0.9)))

or maybe

mytheme <- opts(text = element_text(family="Times", face="plain",
colour="red", size=16, hjust=0.5, vjust=0.5, angle=0, lineheight=0.9))

although the latter would have to either specify everything or fall back
to some defaults for unspecified things.
The advantage of this approach is that it insulates the implementation,
which isn't too hard since there already exists a way of specifying the
structure (using element_*) independent of the implementation.

How deep does relative sizing work?  For instance:

opts(text = element_text(size=16),
      axis.text = element_text(size=rel(0.5)),
      axis.text.x = element_text(size=rel(0.25)))

What would the size of the text on the x axis be?  16*0.5*0.25=2 (rel's
are multiplicative up the tree)? 16*0.5=8 (only the first rel going down
the tree matters and any subsequent ones are ignored)? 16*0.25=4 (only
the last rel in the tree matters, and it is in reference to the last
absolute value)?  I think the first one is what it should be.

In general, I really like the new design. I think it fixes many problems
of the old one, and I don't see any glaringly obvious problems with it.

--
Brian S. Diggs, PhD
Senior Research Associate, Department of Surgery
Oregon Health & Science University

messages.subject: Bug when plotting density plots for groups with one observation
messages.subject_clean: Bug when plotting density plots for groups with one observation
messages.body_plain:
Hi!

I believe I've found one or two bugs in the handling of density plots
in ggplot2. The following code gives a very confusing error message:

$ library(ggplot2)
$ library(plyr)
$
$ movies$decade = round_any(movies$year, 10)
$ ggplot(movies[1:60,], aes(x=rating, colour=decade, group=decade)) +
geom_density(fill=NA)
Error in rowSums(vapply(x, is.finite, logical(nrow(x)))) :
   'x' must be an array of at least two dimensions
Error in UseMethod("scale_dimension") :
   no applicable method for 'scale_dimension' applied to an object of
class "NULL"

I think the reason for the error message is that in rows 1:60, decade
1930 only occurs once:

> table(movies[1:60,]$decade)

1910 1920 1930 1940 1950 1960 1970 1980 1990 2000
    2    2    1    9    2    2    4    7   15   16

It is of course not possible to create a density plot based on only
one observation!

If we include row number 61 (where decade=1930), every thing *appears*
to work fine, i.e., a plot is generated. However, this plot does *not*
contain density estimates for the decades with only two observations;
only five density estimates are shown.

So the problem is that 1) with *one* observation, a confusing error
message is displayed, and 2) with more than one but not enough
observations, no error messages is displayed (but plots for these
groups are not drawn).

I think the best solution would be to draw density plots for the
groups with enough observations, and issue a *warning* (not an error)
if at least one group has too few observations.

messages.subject: Re: geom_smooth for all points
messages.body_plain:
Hi:

Does this work for you?

ggplot(delme, aes(x = doy2, y = NEE_st)) +
   geom_point(aes(colour = as.factor(cod))) +
   geom_smooth(size = 1, colour = 'blue') +
   labs(x = 'Day of year', colour = 'cod') +
   facet_grid(YEAR ~ .) +
   scale_colour_manual(values = c('orange', 'purple'))

I changed the point sizes to reduce the effect of overplotting and the
colors to be friendlier to those with color blindness. To get colors
by cod level but a single overall smooth for a given year, you need to
remove colour as an aesthetic in the top level qplot/ggplot() call and
reserve it for the geom_point() layer, as Brandon showed you. When
colour = is in the top level call, it is assumed to be present in
*all* subsequent layers. In this case, you want color differentiation
in the geom_point() layer but not the geom_smooth() layer, which is
why you don't want colour = in the qplot/ggplot() call.

HTH,
Dennis

Sam

messages.body_plain:
Hi Sam,

Instead of using install_github, download the package source directly and use load_all to load it.  I.e. I grabbed the zip file from https://github.com/hadley/bigvis/zipball/master and unzipped it into ~/R-dev/bigvis  then:

library(devtools)
setwd("~/R-dev/")
load_all("bigvis")

This gets pretty close, without the reference boxes and relative scaling:

library(ggplot2)
library(plyr)
diamonds_sub <- mutate(subset(diamonds, carat < 1.5 & price < 10000),

  price_grid = cut_number(price, 20),
  carat_grid = cut_number(carat, 20))

dia_binned <- bin_nd(diamonds_sub, c("price", "carat", "color"),
  binwidth = c(1000, 0.1, 1))

nbars <- length(dia_binned$centers$color)
dia_binned$centers$color <- 0:(nbars - 1)

dia_glyph <- glyphs(dia_binned, "carat", "color", "price", height = rel(0.9),
  width = nbars/(nbars + 1) * 0.9 * 0.1)

bar_width <- attr(dia_glyph, "width") / (nbars)
glyph_height <- attr(dia_glyph, "height")
dia_glyph <- ddply(dia_glyph, "gid", mutate, total = sum(value))

ggplot(subset(dia_glyph, total > 0)) +

  geom_rect(aes(xmin = gx - bar_width/2, xmax = gx + bar_width/2,
    ymin = price - glyph_height/2 , ymax = gy, fill = factor(color),
                color = factor(color))) +
    xlab("carat") + ylab("price")
